This paper introduces the MultiHuman benchmark, a novel and interesting benchmark for evaluating multi-person image generation models. This dataset addresses the current lack of dedicated multi-person image generation benchmarks, proposes reasonable metrics, and demonstrates the effectiveness of the dataset through extensive experiments.

After extensive discussions between the authors and reviewers, all reviewers recognized the contributions of this paper and agreed to accept it. AC hopes that all comments will be incorporated into the final version.
Thanks for the response to address my concerns. I would like to raise my rating for acceptance.

We highly appreciate your positive evaluation and thoughtful feedback on our work. We are grateful for your recognition of our contributions, particularly the well-designed dataset with 1800 samples and the comprehensive multi-dimensional evaluation metrics. Your constructive suggestions have helped us expand the impact of our benchmark in multi-human image generation research.
We address each of your concerns as follows:
___________________________________________________________________________________________________
### • **W1: Generating Sufficient Number of People Beyond Area Injection**
Count accuracy is a very real limitation that affects all current works in multi-human generation, including MH-OmniGen. Infact, native T2I generation also faces the same issue. This fundamental challenge is clearly demonstrated in Table 4 of the paper, which evaluates the base text-to-image model capabilities for generating accurate human counts. Our findings reveal that diffusion models themselves aren't strong enough to perform this challenging task - even the best performing model (FLUX-Dev) achieves only 63.9% average count accuracy across 1-5 people. Similar to your observation, we found that this represents a critical bottleneck in multi-human generation. Facilitated by our observations in this work and the testbench, we are optimistic that the community will work on this challenge. Here are potential solutions for improving human count which we are currently exploring for future work:

1. Specifically in MH-OmniGen, we update the attention mask to assign unassigned (background) latent pixels to input human faces that haven't found a Hungarian match. In the case where number of generated faces are inaccurate, this pushes the model to generate the human faces in unassigned background regions. However, this approach isn't explicit enough for correct human count generation. A promising (future) direction we are working on is performing spatial sampling in layout to find **non-overlapping** background regions that can be explicitly assigned to each unassigned human. This remains an active area of research, as the technical implementation is non-trivial. Our current results show a promising 1.3 points improvement in count accuracy for this method when the assignment is based on naïve splitting of the unused background region.

2. As shown in Task 2, methods that use spatial priors achieve significantly better human count accuracy. One future direction we are exploring is to implicitly learn spatial priors within T2I models, which breaks down this complex task and makes it more tractable.

3. We designed Task 4 specifically to help researchers developing multi-human generation models select T2I backbones capable of following prompts with specific human counts. This benchmarking approach allows users to evaluate different native T2I models and identify which methods best preserve human count accuracy to build their work upon.

### • **W2: FLUX-Based Comparison Methods**
We appreciate this suggestion and agree that including FLUX-based methods is important for Multi-Human Generation. To clarify, the Regional-PuLiD method in Table 2 of the paper uses Flux as its backbone. Additionally, in Table 4 (Task 4) we have analyzed the native text-to-image generation using Flux backbone. 
During the time of submission, PuLID-Flux + Regional prompting was the only method we found which performs multi-context generation with capability to generate human faces. Recently, Flux-Kontext was released, which can perform in-context generation for a single image. For multiple image inputs, the community suggested image stitching + Flux-Kontext generation. We were able to implement this strategy for Task 2 (as image stitching provides regional priors). The results are summarized below.
| **Backbone** | **Method** | **Count** | **Multi-ID** | **HPS** |
|--------------|------------|-----------|--------------|---------|
| Flux | Regional-PuLID | 67.4 | 50.7 | 26.1 |
| Flux | Flux-Kontext-Dev | 76.8 | 39.2 | 26.9  |
| RV1.5 | UniPortrait | 78.3 | 49.2 | 26.3 |
| SDXL | OMG-InstantID | 71.2 | 32.6 | 27.2 |
| Phi-3 | OmniGen | 77.2 | 48.2 | 27.4 |

Breaking down the numbers, we observe that Flux-Kontext with image stitching performs quite well with lesser number of input faces (1,2) but starts to fail as the number of images increase. There is high scope for improvement with further research on this model as well, such as developing a better strategy as compared to the proposed stitching method.
### • **W3: Unified Evaluation Metric**
Thank you for this suggestion. It is highly valuable for a unified and practical model comparison. We have worked on implementing a unified metric which passes the eye test for images.

We observed that among our 5 metrics, 4 metrics (Accuracy, HPS, Action-S, Action-C) are prompt-image alignment metrics, which measure various aspects such as adherence to action scores and adherence to actions. Likewise, the Hungarian ID similarity is an overall representation of ID matching.

We propose creating a combined metric by taking the **geometric mean** of Multi-ID similarity (which encompasses face similarity per-image) and the average of Count accuracy, HPS and Action scores (which encompasses prompt-image alignment along with image realism across different aspects). The geometric mean formulation is supported by literature which indicates that if one of the two metric components is very low, the overall metric shouldn't be high (as would be the case with simple averaging).

As there are more number of prompt-image alignment metrics, we weigh the prompt-image portion of this geometric mean higher (twice) that of the multi-id similarity portion. Overall, we compute combined score as: 

**Combined Score = (Multi-ID × ((HPS + Action + Accuracy) / 3)^2)^(1/3)**


Here, HPS represents the normalized HPS value with (15, 40) as (min, max). Also note there is a single action score (as the C/S represents the type of input sample (simple/complex)). 
Below are the unified rankings for our top-performing methods on Task 1 (from Table 1 of the paper):

| **Method** | **Multi-ID** | **HPS** | **Action-S** | **Action-C** | **Combined Score** |
|------------|--------------|---------|--------------|--------------|-------------------|
| GPT-Image-1 | 28.8 | 30.3 | 97.0 | 91.1 | 54.3 |
| UniPortrait | 44.2 | 25.9 | 76.2 | 67.2 | 51.7  |
| OmniGen | 49.4 | 26.2 | 87.5 | 71.3 | 59.2  |
| MH-OmniGen | 54.5 | 26.3 | 91.6 | 72.9 | 61.6  |

We will add this metric to our final paper.
### • **W4: Fine-Grained Per-Character Dataset**
We also recognize the value of more granular character-specific descriptions and clothing details. Motivated by your line of thinking, we want to highlight that our current dataset already addresses this to some extent by splitting our prompts into **simple prompts** (describing the overall scene) and **complex prompts** (describing the scene with different actions for individual people). Here are two examples of complex prompts: 

- *"An urban portrait of a total number of Four people waiting at a bus stop: among them, one person is looking at their phone, one person is listening to music, one person is talking, and one person is reading a newspaper."* 

- *"An intimate portrait of a total number of Three people having a serious conversation in the park: among them, one person is standing behind listening intently, one person is gesturing while sitting on the bench, and one person is contemplating."* 

The **Action-C scores** in our results specifically report performance on images generated from these complex prompts. As observed across Tables 1, 2, 3, and 4, current methods show significant room for improvement in these complex scenarios, with most models performing substantially worse on Action-C compared to Action-S metrics. While we are developing extensions that include even more granular character attributes (clothing style, pose, expression) and hierarchical descriptions, our current complex prompt design provides a foundation for evaluating per-character control and compositional understanding in multi-human generation.
___________________________________________________________________________________________________
Please let us know during the discussion period if you have remaining concerns. We will be happy to answer them.

We sincerely thank you for your constructive feedback on our work. We appreciate your recognition of our reasonable evaluation framework and the technical contributions of our Unified Regional Isolation strategies. Your detailed questions and concerns help us clarify important aspects of our methodology and identify areas for improvement.
We address each of your concerns as follows:
__________________________________________________________________________________________________
### • **W1: Pose Image Synthesis and Facial Keypoint Differences**
You raise a valid concern about pose synthesis containing facial keypoints that may differ across identities with varying facial shapes. However, while facial keypoints can indeed be distinct for various faces, current diffusion-based methods (using ControlNet or unified models such as OmniGen) tend to preserve the facial shape of the input reference image instead of fitting to pose keypoints. This behavior persists even when image conditioning on the pose image is high - in our case, ControlNet is conditioned to 1.0 for UniPortrait and OmniGen is set to 2.5 for guidance scale. These methods are often used to maintain human pose and spatial positioning rather than specific facial features from the pose conditioning.

To validate this behavior, we conducted experiments on Task 2 using a subset of 300 images (1, 2, 3 faces) comparing performance with and without facial keypoints. The pose images without facial keypoints were generated for the same scenes as those in our dataset:

| **Method** | **ID Similarity (with facial keypoints)** | **ID Similarity (without facial keypoints)** | **Performance Gap** |
|------------|-------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|-------------------|
| UniPortrait | 56.5 | 56.4 | 0.1 |
| OmniGen | 60.8 | 61.0 | -0.2 |

As demonstrated, the performance gap is minimal in both cases, confirming that facial keypoints in pose images do not significantly impact identity preservation. In our paper, we also show results of Task 1 and Task 2 side by side (with/without our provided poses) in Appendix E.4. Notice that there is no specific trend in Multi-ID metric, and scores do not drop due to facial keypoints.

However, based on your concern, we acknowledge this potential limitation. We want to address the possibility that future methods are designed to preserve facial structures from pose conditioning more aggressively. Hence, we will also open-source and provide the same pose images with and without facial keypoints, along with the rest of the dataset. We have already stored these images for the above experiment. This approach ensures our benchmark remains robust to different types of pose conditioning.

### • **W2: Single-Person Generation in Multi-Human Benchmark**
As discussed in Section 4.2 of the paper, the “Simple prompts” part of our dataset contains images of 1-5 people. We don’t add them to complex prompts, as complex prompts are designed to define different people performing varying actions. We include single human prompts for several important reasons. Many existing works primarily report results on single-face scenarios, and we believe our benchmark should be comprehensive enough, such that this subset can fairly represent and evaluate these methods. Here is an example demonstrating the results of single person action generation on Task 1 for our benchmarked multi-human approaches, and comparing them to PuLID-Flux (which can't natively extend to multi-human):
| **Model** | **ID Similarity** | **HPS** |
|-----------|-------------------|---------|
| PuLID-Flux | 62.9 | 26.3 |
| UniPortrait | 58.2 | 27.0 |
| FastComposer | 28.5 | 19.2 |
| OmniGen | 60.8 | 27.0 |
| GPT-Image-1 | 31.5 | 29.2 |

An interesting point in the above table is that methods trained solely for a single person(such as PuLID) preservation might work better on this task than multi-ID gen models. The challenge of single-person generation remains nuanced and well-founded within the broader multi-human generation framework, as it establishes crucial baselines for identity preservation and prompt adherence. Furthermore, studying the difficulty progression across different numbers of faces provides valuable insights into model capabilities and limitations, and the rate of ID similarity deterioration between 1-5 humans is an interesting way to evaluate SOTA methods.


### • **W3: Handling Occlusion Relationships**
Our proposed approach handles occlusion relationships systematically. For instance, consider Algorithms 1 and 2 for MH-OmniGen in our Appendix. By probing intermediate attention layers and segmenting the base model's predictions, the regions assigned naturally adhere to the occlusion relationships learned by the base model. Each reference image is only assigned to its corresponding unoccluded region, as the segmentation masks from SAM capture the visible portions of each person rather than attempting to generate faces and bodies in occluded areas.

This behavior is visually evident in Figure F.1 (row 2) of our Appendix, where a fireman in the front occludes both people behind. The regions assigned from intermediate SAM masks correctly identify the bodies of all three people, with the front person properly occluding the two in the background. Our Hungarian matching algorithm ensures that each reference image is matched to its visible region without attempting to force generation in occluded areas.

However, we acknowledge that extremely severe occlusion scenarios (where faces are almost entirely hidden) remain a challenging problem (as they do for every other method in Multi-Human Generation). We are exploring enhancements in future work and urge the community to do the same with the help of this benchmark.

### • **W4: MH-OmniGen vs OmniGen for count accuracy**
Thanks for bringing up this point. In Table 1, the slight decrease in Count accuracy for MH-OmniGen (60.3) compared to OmniGen (60.5) occurs in a handful of samples where the OmniGen base model generates extra faces with distorted bodies and/or blended faces. In these same images, MH-OmniGen performs better on ID similarity and HPS/Action scores, demonstrating improved overall generation quality. This trade-off prioritizes a critical challenge of multi-id preservation along with generated image quality and prompt alignment, while reducing subject blending at a minor cost to count accuracy. The 0.2-point decrease is statistically insignificant compared to the substantial 5.1-point improvement in Multi-ID similarity (49.4 → 54.5).


### • **W5: Multi-Perspective Identity Consistency**
Your concern about identity maintenance across different perspectives in Section 4.4 is important for the robustness of our benchmark. PuLID-Flux, which we use for multi-view generation, is specifically trained to preserve identity consistency across different angles through contrastive learning on diverse viewpoints and lighting conditions, making it well-suited for generating the multiple perspectives required for our dataset.

Based on your concern, we conducted a systematic experiment to validate whether our 5 generated views maintain consistent identity representation. We computed cosine similarity of facial embeddings for each of the 5,550 faces across all possible view pairs (5C2 = 10 combinations per face = 55,500 total combinations). The mean ID similarity was 78.5 with a standard deviation of 6.2, which represents excellent identity consistency as similarity scores above 70 consistently pass the eye test for human evaluation.

This multi-view consistency directly translates to improved generation performance. As evidenced in Table 1 and 2 of our paper, Multi-ID similarity scores consistently improved when training with 5 views instead of 1 view - for example, LoRA improved from 17.3 to 21.4, demonstrating that our multi-perspective dataset provides more robust identity representations that enhance model training and evaluation.

### • **W6: Generalizability to Other Generative Models** 
You raise an excellent question about the universality of our proposed techniques. Our Unified Regional Isolation and Implicit Assignment strategies are designed to be model-agnostic and have been successfully applied to different architectures (OmniGen and IR-Diffusion) as demonstrated by MH-OmniGen and MH-IR-Diffusion results. We have since then also implemented the Hungarian Assignment on OMG-InstantID model. MH-OMG-InstantID improves multi-ID similarity from 32.6 to 34.8 in Table 2 of the paper, keeping rest of the scores constant.
The core principles - attention masking for regional isolation and Hungarian matching for assignment - can be adapted to various transformer-based and diffusion architectures. However, implementation details vary depending on the model's attention mechanism and token organization. We provide detailed algorithms (Algorithms 1-3 in Appendix C) to facilitate adaptation to other models. We encourage the community to apply these techniques to additional architectures.

### • **W7: Code Availability**
As verified by other reviewers, we have submitted the code and dataset in the private link during the time of submission. Additionally, we plan to open source the (updated) version of the code after this rebuttal phase. 
__________________________________________________________________________________________________
Please let us know during the discussion period if you have remaining concerns. We will be happy to answer them.

summary.value: This paper introduces a novel benchmark for evaluating generative models in creating images with multiple humans performing complex actions while preserving facial identities. The MultiHuman-Testbench dataset includes 1800 samples with 550 unique human face images, ensuring diversity across age, ethnicity, and gender. It features curated text prompts describing scenes with 1–5 humans, paired with pose conditioning images. The benchmark proposes four metrics: Count Accuracy, Hungarian ID Similarity, Human Preference Score, and Action Detection to assess model performance. The paper evaluates various models, including zero-shot and tuning-based methods, and introduces techniques like regional isolation and Hungarian matching to improve identity preservation. Results show that unified multimodal models like OmniGen perform best, though challenges remain in consistent ID preservation and action accuracy.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The dataset’s 1800 samples and 550 diverse face IDs provide a robust platform for evaluating multi-human image generation, addressing a gap in existing benchmarks focused on single subjects or objects.
2. The dataset ensures diversity across age, ethnicity, and gender, with no minor subjects, and uses stratified sampling for representativeness.
3. The four proposed metrics, including Hungarian ID Similarity using ArcFace embeddings (Page 6), offer a rigorous framework for evaluating complex aspects of multi-human generation.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The data distribution results are obtained by employing LLMs, which is not rigorous for proposing a benchmark. At least manual check should be applied to get the precise results.
2. The image dataset is not released for a better illustration of the benchmark.
3. The manuscript seems to be written in a hurry, many typos should be addressed.

summary.value: This paper introduce MultiHuman test benchmark, a new benchmark for evaluating multi-person image generation models. It contains 1800 samples, with 5550 face images covering different ages, races, and genders, as well as textual prompts and pose-conditioned images. The benchmark evaluates models using four metrics (number of faces, ID similarity, prompt alignment, and action detection), and also proposes new techniques using human segmentation and Hungarian matching to improve ID similarity, providing standardized tools and insights for multi-person image generation research.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. To address the lack of a dedicated benchmark for multi-person image generation, a new benchmark, MultiHuman-Testbench, is proposed.
2. The dataset is well designed: it contains 1800 samples, and the text prompts cover simple to complex human actions.
3.The evaluation metric is well-designed: A multi-dimensional mectirc is proposed, using four key indicators (number of faces, ID similarity, prompt alignment, and action detection) to comprehensively quantify the performance of the generated model in multi-person scenarios.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The current MH-OmniGen  is mainly based on injection into a given area. However, it is a difficult problem to allow the model to generate a sufficient number of people. Are there any potential solutions?
2. The comparison method lacks a FLUX-based solution, which can be supplemented for comparison.
3. The current indicators cover a wide range, and each method has different performance in various aspects. Can we design an indicator that unifies these four aspects and can reasonably compare the effects of different methods?
4.The current prompt describes the entire figure. Can we construct a more fine-grained dataset for each character with different clothes?This may require a new benchmark to complete this new task.

summary.value: This paper proposed a benchmark for the multi-human generation. Measuring multiple humans performing complex actions while preserving their facial identities is the major challenge for the generative model. However, it lacks a concrete metric to measure its generation quality, thereby hindering further improvement. To make a fair comparison, this paper proposed a multi-faceted evaluation suite employing four key metrics to quantify face count, ID similarity, prompt alignment, and action detection. The epxeriment results show that the proposed benchmark could fairly and comprehensive evluate multi-human gneration.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The topic for this paper is vital for the generation task. Currently, diffusion model-based generation suffers from low quality in human generation tasks especially for multi-human generation. A good benchmark could offer a deep insight for the future research.

2. The proposed four metric is sound.

3. The epxeriments show that the proposed benchmark could fairly evluate the generation quality.

limitations_weaknesses.value: 1. The benchmark only contains 1800 samples. The claims said that this benchmark belongs to the large-scale benchmark. However, only containing 1800 samples seems limited for the standard of a large-scale benchmark.

dataset_code_comments.value: The author offers the links to access the entire code and dataset. I have verified the links.

additional_feedback.value: 1. The author may need to enrich the number of samples. To reach the ciaim "large-scale" benchmark, 1800 cases are not enough. It may be better to enrich more samples.

final_justification.value: This paper proposes a benchmark for generating images of multiple humans performing complex actions. This task poses a challenge for current diffusion model-based image generation, thereby enhancing the contribution of this paper. The previous confusion included the scale of the benchmark. After rebuttaling, the author addresses these concerns by illustrating the validity of the samples in the benchmark. However, less than 5k images still limit the scope of the benchmark, and thus I rate it as the boardline accept.

title.value: MultiHuman-Testbench: Benchmarking Image Generation for Multiple Humans

abstract.value: Generation of images containing multiple humans, performing complex actions, while preserving their facial identities, is a significant challenge. A major factor contributing to this is the lack of a a dedicated benchmark. To address this, we introduce MultiHuman-Testbench, a novel benchmark for rigorously evaluating generative models for multi-human generation. The benchmark comprises 1800 samples, including carefully curated text prompts, describing a range of simple to complex human actions. These prompts are matched with a total of 5,550 unique human face images, sampled uniformly to ensure diversity across  age, ethnic background, and gender. Alongside captions, we provide human-selected pose conditioning images which accurately match the prompt. We propose a multi-faceted evaluation suite employing four key metrics to quantify face count, ID similarity, prompt alignment, and action detection. We conduct a thorough evaluation of a diverse set of models, including zero-shot approaches and training-based methods, with and without regional priors. We also propose novel techniques to incorporate image and region isolation using human segmentation and Hungarian matching, significantly improving ID similarity. Our proposed benchmark and key findings provide valuable insights and a standardized tool for advancing research in multi-human image generation.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).
